title: Why China can't fix its broken economy
ticker: Why China can't fix its broken economy: the spending gap, the property hole, and the goods flooding the world

scenes.title: Why China can't fix its broken economy
scenes.say: China's economy grew 4.5 per cent last quarter. On paper, that's fine. But underneath sits a problem Beijing has struggled with for years: Chinese people are not spending enough money.
scenes.speak: China's economy grew four and a half per cent last quarter. On paper, that's fine. But underneath sits a problem Beijing has struggled with for years: Chinese people are not spending enough money.

scenes.title: Consumption in China
scenes.detail: In most economies it is 70% or more
scenes.say: Consumption makes up only about 56 per cent of China's economy. In most countries, it is 70 per cent or more.
scenes.speak: Consumption makes up only about fifty-six per cent of China's economy. In most countries, it is seventy per cent or more.

scenes.title: Consumption, share of GDP
scenes.say: That is about 10 points lower than Japan's was in the 1990s, at the very worst of its lost decade. No major economy in the past 100 years has spent so little of what it makes.
scenes.speak: That is about ten points lower than Japan's was in the nineteen-nineties, at the very worst of its lost decade. No major economy in the past hundred years has spent so little of what it makes.

scenes.title: A model running out of road
scenes.say: Why does it matter? Because low spending is a warning light. It says the model that powered China's rise, build, invest, export, is running out of road.

scenes.title: From double digits to under 5%
scenes.say: Growth topped 10 per cent a year in the early 2000s. This spring it fell to 4.3 per cent, a three-year low, before edging back to 4.5.
scenes.speak: Growth topped ten per cent a year in the early two-thousands. This spring it fell to four point three per cent, a three-year low, before edging back to four point five.

scenes.title: First nine months of 2026
scenes.say: The numbers show the imbalance. Manufacturing grew 5.9 per cent in the last quarter. Retail sales grew just 1.1 per cent this year. The factories are running. The shoppers are not.
scenes.speak: The numbers show the imbalance. Manufacturing grew five point nine per cent in the last quarter. Retail sales grew just one point one per cent this year. The factories are running. The shoppers are not.

scenes.title: The property hole
scenes.say: The biggest drag is housing. For years, a flat was where Chinese families kept their savings. Then the property market broke.

scenes.label: Property investment, Jan–Sept 2026
scenes.say: Investment in property fell 20.6 per cent in the first nine months of this year. Construction shrank. Home prices in the biggest cities are still lower than a year ago.
scenes.speak: Investment in property fell twenty point six per cent in the first nine months of this year. Construction shrank. Home prices in the biggest cities are still lower than a year ago.

scenes.title: Why families hold back
scenes.say: When the main thing you own keeps losing value, you feel poorer. So you save more, and spend less. That deepens the slump.

scenes.title: Where the goods go
scenes.say: But China can't simply make less. Cutting production would mean mass layoffs. So what happens to all the extra stuff? It is sold abroad, more and more of it, at lower and lower prices.

scenes.label: after a record $1.2 trillion in 2025
scenes.say: Exports rose 16 per cent in the first nine months. The trade surplus hit 938 billion dollars, after a record 1.2 trillion last year.
scenes.speak: Exports rose sixteen per cent in the first nine months. The trade surplus hit nine hundred and thirty-eight billion dollars, after a record one point two trillion last year.

scenes.title: 'Dumping'
scenes.say: The technical term for selling abroad below fair value is dumping. And from Europe to Asia, countries say China's surplus is killing their factories.

scenes.title: India–China trade, 2025-26
scenes.say: India feels it directly. Last financial year, India bought 131.6 billion dollars of goods from China and sold it 19.5 billion. A gap of about 112 billion.
scenes.speak: India feels it directly. Last financial year, India bought a hundred and thirty-one point six billion dollars of goods from China and sold it nineteen point five billion. A gap of about a hundred and twelve billion.

scenes.title: Anti-dumping probes in 2026
scenes.say: India's trade remedies office has opened a string of anti-dumping investigations into Chinese goods this year, from electrical steel and forklifts to chemicals and drug ingredients.

scenes.title: Beijing's balancing act
scenes.say: Beijing knows the problem. Fixing it means shifting money from the state and factories to households. That is a delicate balancing act.

scenes.label: Retail sales target, from 50.1 trillion in 2025
scenes.say: In July, China set a goal of 60 trillion yuan in retail sales by 2030, up from 50.1 trillion last year, and promised to significantly raise household spending's share of the economy.
scenes.speak: In July, China set a goal of sixty trillion yuan in retail sales by twenty-thirty, up from fifty point one trillion last year, and promised to significantly raise household spending's share of the economy.

scenes.text: Transitioning to a consumption-led growth model should be the overarching priority.
scenes.say: The IMF agrees. It says moving to growth led by consumption should be China's overarching priority. But targets alone don't change how worried families spend.

scenes.title: For India
items: A bigger Chinese market, if spending grows
scenes.say: For India, the stakes run both ways. If China's shoppers stay home, cheaper goods keep arriving and Indian factories feel the squeeze. If they start spending, China could become a bigger market for Indian exports.

scenes.title: China's problem is everyone's problem
scenes.say: China's spending gap is no longer just China's problem. Until its people buy more, the world will keep buying what they don't.
